description: A small cap whose data business tripled year on year at a 63% margin, priced like the industrial supplier it used to be. Fair value $40 vs $24.
body_html:
A small cap with two businesses the market can’t price together: a 40-year-old industrial franchise that grew into a shrinking market, and a measurement-and-power platform that is 17% of revenue and half of gross profit. The short sellers got their 20% day. I think they got the wrong company.

On a Monday in mid-August a short seller published a report, the stock lost a fifth of its value in a day, and a ten-year contract that had been announced two weeks earlier was gone by the Tuesday. A couple of weeks later, management raised full-year guidance for the second time in five weeks.

You either believe the short report described the business, or you believe the guidance did. The two can’t both be right, and the price today sits closer to the short report.

This piece walks through why I think the guidance is the better description, what the measurement-and-power business is worth on its own, where the bear case is strong, and what my model says a share is worth.

Table of Contents

  • TLDR

  • RankedStocks scorecard

  • Two businesses the market can’t price together

  • The legacy franchise and the contract underneath it

  • The measurement and power platform, unit by unit

  • The industry: three currents, one direction

  • The supply chain, upstream and downstream

  • Financials: what the numbers say and what they hide

  • Returns on capital: eight years below the line

  • Management, the controlling shareholder and governance

  • The bear case, point by point

  • What the market is missing

  • Valuation

  • Verdict

TLDR

  • Flotek Industries [] sells completion chemistry to frac crews (83% of revenue) and sells real-time gas measurement, gas conditioning and rented power generation to the same industry plus utilities and gas-fired plants (17% of revenue but half of gross profit). A ten-year supply agreement with its 58% owner ProFrac [] puts a floor under the chemistry business through May 2032.

  • The bull case: Data Analytics grew 223% in Q2 2026 at a 63% gross margin, 89 XSPCT measurement units are deployed or on order against 25 at year-end 2025, international chemistry in Saudi Arabia is guided to exceed $40M in the second half of 2026 against $11M for all of 2025, and reported EBITDA understates cash earnings by $9M a year because of a non-cash charge nobody adds back.

  • The key risk: ProFrac. It is 57% of revenue, it owes FTK $71M of receivables, it has missed its minimum purchase every period since 2023, and it carries $1.1B of its own debt. If ProFrac stumbles, the chemistry floor cracks.

  • Rating: BUY at a 3.5% weight, the low end of the 3.5-5% range I use for every new position. My DCF gives $40 a share, 67% above the $23.92 close, at an 8.6% WACC and an 11.4x exit multiple on 2036 EBITDA. The bear case is $17, which is 11x consensus 2027 EBITDA. That is 2.3x reward to risk, above my 2x bar.

Trade Alert

I bought FTK 3.5% weight and closed the CCL position locking 22% gain on that one.

As CCL was just 1.6%, I used some more margin (now 5.5% margin on account). It is hard to trim from another position as:

  1. the stories have not played out for some and

  2. the AI-names we have are being unfairly castigated right now and I don’t want to sell in a fear AI-market.

Once I unwind a position(s) to cover the margin I will let you know. It is still under my 20% margin rule.

RankedStocks scorecard

By the way, I have been testing generating AI reports based on the data at RankedStocks.com. Right now it is in BETA, check it out here. Let me know what you think. I am already improving on the automatic DCF and the order of sections (eg. moving the SWOT to the top…etc).

FTK scores 85 out of 100 on RankedStocks.com, ahead of 96% of US stocks and 96% of its US peers, and it has held the Elite range (80 and above) for 77 days, since the July breakout.

RankedStocks is free, and each factor below opens on the metrics behind it.

Valuation, 12. FTK trades at 17.7x trailing and 20.2x forward EBITDA, 24.2x trailing and 30.0x forward earnings, and 5.8x invested capital, which puts it in the most expensive eighth of 298 US materials stocks. The forward multiples sit above the trailing ones because consensus has EPS falling 5.2% next year as the shortfall fees roll off, even with EBITDA growing 42.8%. Price to cash flow is negative because operating cash flow over the last twelve months was -$2.2M.

Growth, 84. Over the last twelve months revenue grew 36.8%, EBITDA 103.3%, operating cash flow 114.3% and ROIC 90.6%. On a forward basis revenue growth is 51.4% and EBITDA growth 42.8%. The weak lines are per share: forward EPS growth is -5.2% and the long-term estimate is 4.6%, which is where the end of the shortfall fees and the contract-asset amortisation show up.

Profitability, 70. Trailing ROIC is 19.3%, ROE 32.3% and return on total capital 20.6%, on capex of 1.0% of sales and asset turnover of 1.09. Gross margin is 24.5%, EBITDA margin 17.7% and net margin 13.0%. Cash is the weak side: levered free cash flow margin is -1.7%, trailing operating cash flow -$2.2M and the five-year average ROIC -32.9%, the history the returns section explains.

Sentiment, 92. Thirteen analysts cover FTK: seven rate it Buy and six Hold, with no Sells.

The consensus target is $34.50, 44% above the $23.92 close, with a median of $32, a high of $44 and a low of $27.50.

Outlook, 95. The June quarter, brought $99.4M of revenue against a $69.5M estimate and $0.26 of EPS against $0.13. Revenue has beaten the estimate in each of the last seven reports…

… while EPS missed in two of the last eight.

Two businesses the market can’t price together

Picture a frac site in the Delaware Basin at three in the morning. Twenty pumps, each the size of a truck, pushing sand and water down a well at 10,000 psi. Those pumps used to burn diesel. More and more of them burn natural gas from a nearby well, because a crew that switches saves up to $10M a year in fuel. The trouble is that field gas is not a product. Its heating value swings 20-25% from one stage to the next, it carries liquids, and when a slug of heavy gas reaches an engine the engine knocks, derates or shuts down. A shutdown on a frac spread costs the operator the whole crew’s day rate.

Flotek sells two things to that site. The first is the chemistry that goes down the well: friction reducers, surfactants and its “Complex nano-Fluid” additives, blended to the well’s geology under what it calls Prescriptive Chemistry Management. The second is a box that reads the gas every few seconds, blends it to a stable fuel, and splits it across the engines. That second box is the seed of a business that did not exist in Flotek’s numbers two years ago and produced half the company’s gross profit in Q2 2026.

The market has to decide which company it is looking at, and markets prefer to think in binary. At 17.7x trailing EBITDA, RankedStocks scores FTK 12.2 out of 100 on valuation, close to Solaris Energy Infrastructure [] at 2.7, the pure play on rented power for data centers, and well below the frac-exposed names, Halliburton [] at 27.8 and ProFrac at 79.9. So the price already says “power company”. But the short report and the August selloff treated it as a frac supplier that had just lost its growth story. Both views are half right.

The legacy franchise and the contract underneath it

Flotek’s chemistry business is 40 years old and spent most of the last decade shrinking.

Revenue fell from $449M in 2014 to $43M in 2021 after it sold its citrus-terpene processing arm to ADM [] for $175M and lost its way in the 2020 downturn. What saved it was ProFrac.

In February 2022 ProFrac, the pressure pumper controlled by the Wilks family, signed a ten-year chemical supply agreement and paid for it with $60M of convertible notes. The agreement obliges ProFrac to buy the greater of 70% of its chemistry needs or a 30-fleet baseline from Flotek, and if it falls short it pays liquidated damages equal to 25% of the shortfall. The notes converted in 2023 and ProFrac became the majority holder. Revenue went from $43M in 2021 to $237M in 2025.

The agreement has two features that matter more than the headline.

First, ProFrac has missed the minimum every period. Shortfall fees were $20M in the second half of 2023, $32M in 2024 and $27M in 2025, and they carry close to 100% margin because nothing ships against them. Strip them out and 2025 chemistry gross margin was about 8%, not the 20% that the reported number shows, and 2024 was closer to 3%. That is the earnings-quality point the bears make, and it is a fair one. The answer to it sits in the 2026 numbers: Q2 chemistry gross margin was 13% with only $1.2M of fees inside it, the first time the underlying product margin has been in double digits since the ProFrac agreement began. ProFrac ran 22 active fleets at year-end 2025 against the 30-fleet baseline written into the contract, which is why it keeps missing the minimum.

Second, Flotek booked the $83M of consideration it paid ProFrac as a contract asset and amortises it as a reduction of revenue: $6.3M in 2025, $9M in 2026, $9.9M in 2027, $10.2M a year in 2028-2030 and $12.8M a year to May 2032. The company used to add that back to Adjusted EBITDA. It stopped. So the $50-54M guided for 2026 is after a $9M non-cash deduction that no competitor carries. I’ll come back to this in valuation, because it is worth $1.30 a share on its own.

US frac activity fell through the first half of 2026: Primary Vision’s spread count bottomed at 145 in February, down from 202 a year earlier, and only recovered to 199 by mid-October. Flotek grew chemistry revenue 26% in Q1 and posted its strongest chemistry quarter since 2017 in Q2 into that decline. Three things did it: external domestic chemistry rose 43%, international went from $3.9M to $10.6M, and ProFrac’s own fleet stayed active while others parked.

The international line is the swing factor for 2026. Saudi Aramco [2222.SR] started production at Jafurah, the largest unconventional gas field outside North America, in December 2025 and targets 2 Bcf/d of sales gas by 2030 on more than $100B of lifecycle investment. Flotek is on four frac fleets there with a path to six by year-end under a contract with more than four years of scope. The CEO’s words on the Q2 call: “we’re on 4 frac fleets in the Jafurah field, providing chemistry... We have that potential of that business to expand to 6 by the end of the year.” Half-year international revenue was $12.6M. The September guidance says the second half could exceed $40M. That is a tripling in six months, and it is the number Q3 will test.

A Houston chemistry company that struggles to take share from Halliburton at home can win in Saudi Arabia because the two markets buy chemistry in different ways. In the US, the big pumpers make their own friction reducer and chemistry is a low-margin commodity they control; Liberty Energy [] said in July that “sand and chemical margins remained challenged despite high volumes”. In a NOC tender the chemistry is specified and bought separately, and a company with 130 patents and a 20,000-well database can qualify as a supplier on its own merits. That is why I treat Jafurah as durable, though the Q3 print has to show it.

The second chemistry story is smaller but tells you where the company is going. Flotek now installs its optical analyzers on the crude coming out of the well and uses the readings to tune the chemistry going in. One operator identified 1-6% more production within 60 days and extended the program to other pads.

A chemistry supplier that can show the operator the barrels its additive produced can price on those barrels instead of on gallons shipped.

The measurement and power platform, unit by unit

Data Analytics is the reason to own the stock. It has three products, and they share one piece of technology: an optical spectrometer, built in-house by the JP3 team Flotek bought in 2020, that reads a gas or liquid stream every five to twenty seconds without a shelter, a calibration gas or a technician.

XSPCT: digital valuation of gas. When gas changes hands at a custody-transfer point, both sides agree a price per MMBtu, and the heating value is measured by a gas chromatograph that samples every few minutes and needs a climate-controlled shelter and calibration gas. XSPCT reads the stream every few seconds. In nine months of trials across three basins it matched the chromatograph to within 0.3 BTU per cubic foot, and in November 2025 it became the first optical instrument certified to the GPA 2172 custody-transfer standard. Deployed-or-contracted units went from 25 at year-end 2025 to 57 in March and 89 in June.

The market it sells into is the $7.9B process-analyzer business that Emerson [ ], ABB [ABBN], Siemens [SIE], Yokogawa [6841.T] and Honeywell [] share, growing 5% a year, and the number of points where gas quality has to be certified is rising. North American LNG export capacity goes from 11.4 Bcf/d in 2023 to 24.4 Bcf/d by 2028 as Plaquemines, Corpus Christi Stage III, Golden Pass, Rio Grande and Port Arthur come on, and every train and every feed pipeline is a custody-transfer point that needs a heating value it can defend.

The customer economics let this scale. Flotek’s own example: at $2.50 per MMBtu and 15 million cubic feet a day, a producer who finds the 20-25% swings in heating value that a chromatograph averages away, and gets paid for the liquids that “dry gas” wells carry, picks up $4.4M a year per site.

Flotek does not disclose what it charges per unit. Nobody outside the company has that number, so I triangulated it. Data Analytics product revenue was $5.2M in Q2 and service revenue $14.0M; the service line includes the $6.8M ProFrac lease and $5.9M from the Montana contract, which leaves $1-2M a quarter of service revenue across the installed analyzer base, or on the order of $50-80K a unit a year on a data-as-a-service basis. If the customer value is $4.4M a year, a $60K subscription is a 1-2% take rate. That ratio is why management can talk about 200,000 potential US locations with a straight face, and why I expect pricing to rise as the installed base proves the number.

VeraCal: flare monitoring. The EPA’s OOOOb methane rule required continuous heating-value monitoring on flares by June 2026, and VeraCal is EPA-certified for it. The April 2026 reconsideration broadened the exemptions, raised the temporary flaring allowance from 24 to 72 hours and set up a second rollback by year-end. Congress repealed the Waste Emissions Charge rule in March 2025 and the July 2025 budget law pushed the charge itself out to 2034, so the flare-monitoring case now rests on economics. VeraCal was $2.2M of 2025 revenue at a 60% margin. I model nothing special for it.

PWRtek: the gas-to-power stack. It is the largest of the three by revenue. In April 2025 Flotek bought from ProFrac 30 mobile gas conditioning and distribution units, their inventory and their patents, for $107.5M, paid in a 6M-share warrant, a $40M note and offsets against shortfall fees, then leased the units back to ProFrac for six years at a fixed $27.4M a year through April 2030. That lease alone is $13.7M of half-year revenue at a gross margin near 90%. On the $105M Flotek paid, $27.4M of rent is a 26% cash yield and a four-year payback, about $76K a month per skid, with $104.9M of rent still contracted through April 2030.

The equipment answers the three-in-the-morning problem from the opening. A measurement skid reads BTU, methane number, water and H2S; a conditioning skid knocks out liquids and blends CNG into the field gas to hold the methane number steady; distribution skids give each engine its own regulated feed. In the case study below, on a 40 MW spread, the platform held a 66 methane number with zero engine events, ran 92% field-gas substitution, and the customer counted $3.1-5.5M a year of fuel, maintenance and uptime savings against a rental that returns six to ten times its cost.

If the customer’s return is 6-10x, Flotek’s rental on a 40 MW site is $300-900K a year for a set of skids that cost a few hundred thousand dollars to build and are made in four to five weeks. Management said there are 110-120 gas-fired fleet locations in the US, each 35-40 MW, that it has measurement on 75 of them, and that “revenue per location increases dramatically” when a site upgrades from measurement to control and distribution. The CEO put the measured or controlled capacity at close to 5 GW by Q1 2027 once a gas-fired plant project is counted. If 40 of the 75 measured sites upgrade to full conditioning at $500K a year, that is $20M of new high-margin rental revenue against a Data Analytics base of $63M this year.

The same stack works outside the oilfield, which is where the stock got expensive and then got hit. In March 2026 Flotek won its first utility contract: up to 50 MW of rented generation for a federal disaster-recovery site, six months with a four-year extension option, framed at $1M per MW for the first six months. Phase 1 was 12 MW and brought $5.9M in Q2. Then the generation was paused on infrastructure delays, Phase 2 is unsigned, and guidance assumes nothing from it in Q4. On the call the CFO was clear the extension would run at “$6M per quarter” if it comes, and that rented generation carries lower margins than owned equipment.

Then came Puerto Rico. On August 3 Flotek announced a ten-year award to supply up to 40 MW of generation and smart skids within a 400 MW gas project for PREPA, the island’s utility, worth $40M a year. On August 14 Puerto Rico’s fiscal oversight board revoked the underlying contract of about $6B with the consortium lead, Power Expectations, and referred it to law enforcement. On August 17 Wolfpack Research published a short report. On August 18 PREPA terminated.

The industry: three currents, one direction

Flotek sits at the intersection of three markets, and all three are moving its way in 2027 even if 2026 was a trough for one of them.

US completions. Rigs crossed 600 in October for the first time since May 2024, with 603 US rigs and 272 in the Permian.

The frac spread count is 199, up 24 from a year ago. The EIA’s October outlook has Brent at $96 for 2026 and $84 for 2027 with Middle East supply still constrained, and Henry Hub at $3.48 and $3.16. Rystad expected 8-12 incremental frac fleets by year-end and 18-25% frac price inflation at $85-90 oil. For Flotek, more fleets mean more chemistry volume and, because almost every new fleet burns gas, more gas-conditioning sites. Patterson-UTI [] says 80% of the equipment it offers burns natural gas, and ProFrac, Patterson and ProPetro [] each retired 330,000-400,000 horsepower of diesel pumps in 2024.

The fleet count understates the chemistry those fleets consume. The average Permian lateral went from 6,149 feet in 2015 to 10,867 feet in 2025, and wells longer than 15,000 feet were 15% of last year’s completions. Horizontal completions have held near 6,000 a year since 2022, so the same number of wells pumps more stages, more water and more friction reducer every year. Water is the other multiplier. The Permian produces about 22 million barrels of water a day, three and a half barrels for every barrel of oil, and only 25-30% of it is recycled into new fracs, with Diamondback [] targeting 65% and Devon [] 50%. Recycled water is salty, salty water needs salt-tolerant friction reducers and scale inhibitors, and that is the corner of the chemistry menu where a supplier with a 20,000-well database earns a margin.

Middle East unconventional gas. Jafurah is a 229 Tcf resource that Aramco plans to take from 450 MMcf/d today to 2 Bcf/d by 2030. Halliburton won a multi-year stimulation contract there in July as part of a multi-billion-dollar framework. Every stage that gets fracked needs chemistry, and in Saudi Arabia the chemistry is tendered on its own. If you read my NESR deep dive, you know why I like being paid by the world’s lowest-cost producer to help it grow volumes. Flotek is the chemistry leg of the same trade.

Behind-the-meter power. Grid Strategies’ latest load-growth report puts five-year US peak demand growth at 166 GW, up from 24 GW in its 2022 edition, with data centers 90 GW of it. Enverus forecasts 25.5 GW of new behind-the-meter industrial demand in 2026-2030, 88% from data centers, needing 29.6 GW of gas-fired generation: 7.1 GW of reciprocating engines and 6.2 GW of small turbines. Utility-scale turbines are sold out into 2028-2029, so the near-term answer is engines and small turbines that run on whatever gas is nearby. Those are the machines that knock on dirty gas.

Berkeley Lab counts 2,061 GW of generation waiting for a grid connection at the end of 2025, gas projects up 86% in a year to 253 GW, and a median wait of more than five years from request to operation. GE Vernova’s [] gas-turbine backlog and reservations reached 116 GW in the second quarter and it is booking deliveries for 2031; Caterpillar’s [] power customers are ordering through 2030 against a $72B backlog. Behind-the-meter gas and fuel-cell capacity tied to data centers passed 12 GW by mid-2026 from under 3 GW at the start of 2025.

The unit economics of rented gas power are public from the larger players and they bound what Flotek can earn. Liberty guides to $1.5M of capex per MW, a five-to-six-year payback and 17-18% unlevered returns on ten-year contracts. Solaris shows 18-20% unlevered IRRs on a $600M, 300 MW build and plans 3.2 GW by 2029.

Solaris’s second-quarter numbers put that in rental terms: $158M of power revenue on about 950 MW earning, or about $55K per MW a month at a 61% segment margin. Flotek’s conditioning case study, $3.1-5.5M a year of customer savings on 40 MW, is $6-11 per kW a month of value delivered for a rental that costs the customer a tenth of that, which is why conditioning is the higher-margin, lower-capital corner of the same market. Kodiak Gas Services [] earns a 64.5% gross margin on 363 revenue-generating MW and just signed a six-year, 76 MW data-center deal using 40 reciprocating engines. Engines and aeroderivatives cost $1,700-2,000 per kW installed with 15-36 month lead times.

With 30 skids, a 50 MW utility job and $13M of cumulative capex, an $865M company won’t take on Liberty, Solaris, VoltaGrid and Kodiak as a prime generator. It fits as the instrument and conditioning supplier to all of them, the way a pressure-pumping boom made money for the sand and chemistry suppliers before it made money for the pumpers. Every one of those 29.6 GW needs its fuel measured and conditioned, and the field-gas problem gets worse as the engines move from the Permian to data center campuses run by people who have never seen a methane number.

The supply chain, upstream and downstream

What Flotek buys. The chemistry raw materials are commodity polymers and surfactant feedstocks. Polyacrylamide, the friction-reducer polymer, has sat at $1.63-1.82 per kg through 2026 and US guar gum at $1,440-1,630 per tonne; neither is squeezing margins, and the polymer supply is deepening rather than tightening: SNF, the largest producer, is spending $375M to expand its Plaquemine, Louisiana complex, with oilfield friction reducers the main product.

The citrus terpene that gives the nano-fluid line its name comes from orange oil, a by-product of juice pressing, and here the supply picture is worse: USDA’s October forecast has the Florida crop at 10M boxes, 23% lower year on year and 4% of its 1998 peak, and Brazil’s crop 10% lower with greening in half the trees.

Flotek flags “crop dependent raw materials” as a risk but says they are “generally available on the open market from multiple sources”. Its top supplier was 25% of 2025 spend and 34% in the second quarter of 2026, and the optical components inside the analyzers are sole-sourced. Finished-goods inventory went from $9.7M at year-end to $24.8M at June 30 as product was staged for Saudi Arabia, which is where the working capital went. The hardware in PWRtek, engines and turbines, comes from the OEMs; Flotek’s own content is the skid, the sensor, the control software and the patents.

Who Flotek sells to. ProFrac was 62% of revenue in 2024 and 2025 and 57% in Q2 2026. The next layer is the external pumpers and E&Ps that buy chemistry and rent measurement, then the midstream and gas-plant customers for XSPCT and the utilities for power. International revenue is booked in the UAE through a supply-chain partner even though the work is in Saudi Arabia, which is why no filing names Aramco. The $12.5M equipment credit from the 2025 shortfall settlement obliges Flotek to buy its next Data Analytics equipment from ProFrac’s own fabrication shop, so the supplier and the customer are the same group for part of the capex.

Who else sells into the chain. On chemistry, the SLB [] and ChampionX combination (closed July 2025 for $7.8B), Halliburton and Baker Hughes [] in-house, and Innospec [], whose oilfield unit grew 14% in Q2 with a 32% gross margin. On measurement, Emerson’s Daniel and Honeywell’s Enraf lines own custody transfer with chromatographs; ABB too. On power, the names above. Flotek is small against every one of them, which is both the risk and the reason a 50-unit order moves the needle.

Financials: what the numbers say and what they hide

Revenue grew from $43M in 2021 to $237M in 2025 and is guided to $360-370M this year. Gross margin went from 7.5% in 2021 to 25.2% in 2025, helped by shortfall fees, and sits at 22% in my 2026 model as the fees fade and lower-margin rental power enters the mix. Q2 2026 was the best quarter in a decade: revenue $99.4M, up 70%, net income $10.0M, Adjusted EBITDA $16.8M, up 109%, and the shortfall fee inside those numbers was only $1.2M against $7.8M a year earlier. The growth is organic now.

The cash flow hides the working capital. Receivables rose from $83M at year-end 2025 to $114M at June 30, and ProFrac owed $70.7M of it. Operating cash flow was negative $6.6M in the first half on $14.6M of net income. The CFO said on August 5 that the ABL had been repaid to zero since quarter-end because “we’ve monetized a lot of the receivables that we built up there at the end of the quarter”. Q3 will show whether that is true, and it is the first thing I will check on November 3.

Balance sheet. At June 30 Flotek had $4.4M of cash, $10.4M on its ABL and the $40M 10% PWRtek note, for net debt of $46M, under 1x this year’s EBITDA. On September 23 it replaced that with a $120M senior secured term loan: $75M funded at close, $15M of delayed draw to mid-2027, $30M more by March 2028 with lender consent, maturing September 2031, no amortisation for two years. The 8-K puts the rate at SOFR plus 6.5% with a 2.5% floor, which is 10.3% today, with a 1.3x minimum-return make-whole and a covenant capping debt at 3x EBITDA. The loan refinances the PWRtek note and funds Data Analytics equipment. That is the right use of money at a 6-10x customer return, and the wrong rate to pay for long. My model assumes it refinances toward 8% once net debt turns to net cash, which happens in 2028 on my numbers; every point of permanent debt cost above that is worth $1.20 a share.

Taxes. Flotek has $184.6M of federal NOLs, but a Section 382 ownership change in 2023 caps the use of the pre-change pool at $3.5M a year plus a $24.5M built-in gain, so cash taxes will converge on the 25-26% book rate faster than the headline NOL suggests. I use the book rate.

Returns on capital: eight years below the line

The test I care about most is whether a company earns more on its capital than that capital costs, which is why I put ROIC ahead of ROE.

Flotek failed that test in eight of the last ten years. RankedStocks counts only 2023 and 2025 above the cost of capital, with a five-year average spread of -41 points and a 2025 spread of +13 points.

Three things kept it below the line.

The first is the product. In the US the big pumpers blend their own friction reducer, so an outside chemistry supplier sells a commodity to customers who can make it themselves, and its prices follow raw-material costs with a lag.

The second is the shrink. Revenue went from $317M in 2017 to $43M in 2021, through the sale of the citrus-terpene arm and the 2020 downturn, while the plants and the overhead stayed. Gross margin was negative from 2020 to 2022, and ROIC was worse than -95% in each of those three years.

The third is the cost of the rescue. The ProFrac agreement brought volume in 2022, but it also lifted invested capital from $33M to $122M in a year when gross margin was still below zero.

Flotek crossed the line in 2023 on the first shortfall fees, sat near the cost of capital in 2024 and crossed it again in 2025. The 2025 return, 16.5% in my model and 13 points above WACC on RankedStocks, needs two adjustments before you believe it. The first takes it down. The $27.4M of 2025 shortfall fees earned close to 100% margin; strip them out and ROIC was near zero. I keep them in, because the contract was written to pay Flotek the gross profit ProFrac didn’t order, and ProFrac paid. The second adjustment also takes it down. Because Flotek and ProFrac are under common control, the $107.5M PWRtek purchase was booked at ProFrac’s $14.9M carrying value and the $92.6M difference went to equity, so assets that earn $27.4M of rent sit on $23M of PP&E. Put the $92.6M back and 2025 ROIC is 9.6%, a point above the cost of capital, and 2026 is about 13% against the 20% the book numbers show. On the money Flotek paid, the lease earns about 20% pre-tax after $4M of depreciation and running cost: a good deal, and the fixed rent ends in April 2030.

I expect the spread to hold because of the mix. Data Analytics earns a 63% gross margin, its rentals pay back in about four years, and Flotek’s content in each skid is the sensor, the software and the patents, so each dollar of capital carries a lot of revenue. Chemistry product margin without fees went from about 3% in 2024 to 13% in Q2 2026, and the model has sales to capital at 2.2x this year. The model then lets ROIC fade to 14% by 2037 as capital builds faster than revenue.

That fade is deliberate. A 5.6-point spread over the cost of capital in 2037 is what pays for the 11.4x exit multiple; if ROIC fell to the cost of capital, growth would add no value and the multiple would fall toward the 8.5x of my stress case. Three things could close the spread sooner: the 2030 lease reprice, the end of fee protection in 2032, and more rented generation like Montana, where Flotek passes through third-party engines at a small markup.

Management, the controlling shareholder and governance

Dr. Ryan Ezell became CEO in June 2023 after two years as President; the shares have risen 544% since.

He is a chemist by training, ran fluids at Halliburton before Flotek, and the company he describes on calls, “measure more”, is a different company from the one that came within a going-concern note of failing in 2022.

The CFO joined in December 2022 and has delivered four straight years of rising Adjusted EBITDA and a clean audit after the material weaknesses of 2022. Capital allocation since 2023 has been sound: the PWRtek purchase was financed without cash, the 2025 shortfall was settled in cash plus equipment Flotek wanted anyway, and cumulative capex on the measurement fleet is $13M for a business producing $20M a quarter.

ProFrac owned 58% of the shares at June 30, 61% counting the 2.2M pre-funded warrants, and has the right to name four of seven directors. In September ProFrac moved a $60M block of FTK shares to two Wilks-family entities to cancel $60M of its own term loans; the Wilks complex still controls the company. Every major transaction of the last four years, the supply agreement, the convertibles, the PWRtek purchase at 7x book value, the lease-back, the $40M note later assigned to a Wilks-affiliated lender, the equipment credit, has had ProFrac on the other side.

Conflicts of interest may occur, but I think the independent chairman, KPMG and a parent guarantee on the lease are the counterweights. I don’t see value having been taken from minorities in the record so far, but you are a passenger.

The bear case, point by point

1. ProFrac is the business, and ProFrac is stretched.

ProFrac lost $74.7M in Q2 2026 on $498M of revenue, burned $7.9M of FCF, carries $1.1B of principal debt against $18.8M of cash, and runs 3.9x net debt to annualised EBITDA. It has missed its chemistry minimum every period, owes Flotek $71M, and settled part of last year’s shortfall with equipment rather than cash. If ProFrac restructures, the floor under the chemistry business becomes a claim in a restructuring.

My answer: ProFrac affirmed covenant compliance, has no going-concern language, refinanced its ABL in July, and its chemistry purchases from Flotek rose in dollars even as the shortfall fee shrank, which means the fleets are running. The receivable is the real exposure, and it is why I want Q3 operating cash flow. A ProFrac restructuring is the one scenario that takes the stock below my bear case.

2. The margin story was shortfall fees.

2025 EBITDA of $32.8M included $27.4M of fees at close to 100% margin.

My answer: true for 2025, not for 2026. Q2 fees were $1.2M and EBITDA doubled anyway. The 2026 guide of $50-54M carries perhaps $5M of fees. The margin story is now Data Analytics mix.

3. The power story has no power.

Montana is paused and unextended. PREPA is gone. The company’s own new risk factor concedes “limited operating history in providing infrastructure-scale power generation services” and that for PREPA 90% of the generation would have come from third parties. The “>$1B pipeline” is bids with no signed contracts behind them.

My answer: I model no PREPA and no Montana Phase 2 in 2026, and Data Analytics growing 32% in 2027 against 223% in Q2. The base case needs one Montana-sized award a year, and the measurement base of 75 sites and 89 XSPCT units is already installed.

4. Wolfpack.

On August 17 Wolfpack Research published its short report and the stock fell about 20%, its worst day since March 2020. The report made five claims. The $400M PREPA deal had been cancelled and Flotek hadn’t told shareholders. The deal was about 57% of near-term backlog, and the stock had risen 35% on the award. The oversight board’s concerns were public by August 7, and Flotek kept promoting the contract. Flotek had skipped basic diligence on its partner: Power Expectations reported $17M of revenue against a project the board valued at $1.2B a year, Wolfpack says its CEO has a 2015 felony conviction (he denies wrongdoing), and the signature that bound the original partner, Enchanted Rock, came from a man local media identified as having pleaded guilty in a fraud case. And the August guidance, Wolfpack said, leaned on PREPA. Securities class actions followed, with an October 26 lead-plaintiff deadline.

My answer: two of the claims hold. The backlog point is right, and the backlog slide in the power section shows it. The diligence point is fair too: Flotek joined the consortium on July 31 as a substitute for Enchanted Rock, a week before the board’s concerns went public, and a 40 MW award inside a $6B emergency contract led by a $17M company deserved more scepticism than it got, from management and from the buyers who took the stock up 35%. The guidance claim is wrong. The $340-350M guide issued on August 4 excluded any PREPA contribution, Flotek said on August 18, and three weeks later the company raised it to $360-370M, still without PREPA. No equipment shipped, no revenue was booked and no capex was spent. The disclosure timing is for the courts. If discovery shows Flotek knew the award was unsound when it announced it, the governance discount should be larger than the one I use, and I can’t rule that out. The stock rose 35% on a story and fell 20% when the story broke; neither move changed the 75 sites and 89 analyzers already in the field.

5. The 2032 cliff and the 2030 reprice.

The supply agreement’s minimum-purchase protection ends in May 2032 and the PWRtek lease goes to market rate in its sixth year from April 2030. The valuation-allowance release in 2025 was supported only by income contracted through those dates.

My answer: both are in the model: the lease falls to $13.7M in 2032 and $14-15M after, and I grow ProFrac chemistry at the fleet count, not at the contract. A DCF with 69% of value in the terminal year is still a DCF about what the company looks like after the contracts, and that is a fair criticism of any growth stock.

6. Dilution and the warrant overhang.

Diluted shares went from 12M in 2022 to 38M. ProFrac holds 2.2M pre-funded warrants at a tenth of a cent.

My answer: the dilution bought the contract, the equipment and survival. I count the warrants as shares, $54M of value at today’s price, in every per-share number here. There are no more in the drawer; the 6M warrant from the PWRtek deal was exercised in March.

7. It is already expensive.

RankedStocks scores FTK 12.2 out of 100 on valuation, at 17.7x trailing and 20.2x forward EBITDA and 30.0x forward earnings. At $23.92 the enterprise value, counting the warrants, is about $965M, or 18.6x the midpoint of this year’s EBITDA guide.

My answer: on my 2027 EBITDA of $60M the multiple is 16.1x, and on cash EBITDA, adding back the $9.9M amortisation, it is 13.8x, for a business growing revenue 11% and EBITDA 25%. Solaris scores 2.7 on valuation for 30% forward revenue growth. FTK is priced between a chemical supplier and a power company, and its forward growth of 11.6% sits between them too.

8. Saudi is a stocking order.

Half-year international was $12.6M; the guide needs more than $40M in the second half. Inventory went up $16.6M in six months.

My answer: this is the most honest doubt on the list and the one the Q3 print settles. Four fleets with a path to six, under a contract with four years of scope, in a field going from 0.45 to 2 Bcf/d, is not a stocking order; but a $40M half with in-transit inventory is a timing bet, and if it slips the stock will trade down on the day.

What the market is missing

Ten articles have been published on FTK on Seeking Alpha since October 2024. Seven say the thesis is the Data Analytics mix shift and seven say the risk is ProFrac. They are right on both.

Reported EBITDA understates cash earnings by $9-13M a year. The contract-asset amortisation from the legacy section is 17% of the 2026 EBITDA guide, the company no longer adds it back, and adding it back is worth $1.30 a share.

Half the gross profit comes from 17% of revenue, and the market still screens the company as a chemical supplier. Most quant screens will show a 24% gross margin business tied to the rig count. The segment data shows a 63% gross margin business growing 223% bolted to it. That is why the short-interest number is 25% of the float, and why the free float is only 15M shares; a company that looks like two different things attracts both sides.

The attach-rate math on gas-fired fleets. Flotek measures 75 of 110-120 sites, and each one is worth more once it upgrades to full conditioning. It is the cheapest growth in the model because the sales call has already happened.

The chemistry business is more international than the filings let on. The 10-K says less than 10% of revenue is outside the US. By Q2 it was 10.4% in a single quarter and guided to a run-rate near 25% of chemistry in the second half. A chemistry franchise selling into NOC tenders deserves a different multiple from one selling to Permian pumpers that make their own friction reducer.

Share Beating The Tide: Stock Picks That Outperform

Valuation

You can check out the full model here.

I value FTK on a ten-year DCF with an exit multiple. The model is built from the segments up.

Revenue. 2026 at $367M, the guidance midpoint, with ProFrac flat in the second half, international at $53M and Data Analytics at $63M. Chemistry grows 6.7% in 2027 and fades to 2.6%, below the 3.4% market growth less some share loss to in-house blending. Data Analytics grows 32% in 2027, then fades by three points a year to 4.2% by 2037, which takes it to $83M next year, $208M in 2031 and 43% of revenue by 2037. For scale, $208M in 2031 is the ProFrac lease, Montana-sized utility work every year, the attach-rate step-up and 300 to 400 XSPCT units. It needs no PREPA.

Margins. Chemistry gross margin 13.5-14% with no shortfall fees after 2026. Data Analytics 63% this year and 60% thereafter, as rented generation dilutes the 90% lease margin. Mix takes company gross margin from 22% to 29% by 2031 and 33% by 2037. SG&A falls from 8.4% of revenue to 7% on scale. EBITDA margin goes from 13% to 21% in 2031 and 26% by 2037; EBITDA is $48M this year (the $52M guide less stock compensation), $60M in 2027, $128M in 2031 and $215M in 2036.

Cash flow. Capex 5.5-6% of revenue in 2026-27 for the measurement and conditioning fleet, fading to 3.5%. Receivables from 105 days to 90 by 2031 and 75 by 2037 as the mix moves away from ProFrac. The $9-13M of contract-asset amortisation added back through May 2032. Interest at 10.5% on the term loan until 2027, 8% from 2031. Tax at the 25% book rate.

Discount rate and terminal value. An 8.6% WACC from a 0.79 unlevered beta for oilfield services and equipment, a 9.4% cost of equity, an 8% long-term cost of debt and a 25% target debt-to-capital. The exit multiple is derived from the model’s own 2036 margins, capex and 3% growth, and comes out at 11.4x EBITDA, in line with where SLB, Innospec and Select Water Solutions [] trade today. Terminal value is 69% of enterprise value.

The result is $40 a share, 67% above the $23.92 close. The reverse DCF says the same thing from the other side: today’s price discounts about a 10% annual return on these cash flows, or 29% a year of free-cash-flow growth for ten years from the depressed 2025 base, with no terminal growth.

What moves it. Each lever, holding everything else:

Three points a year of extra Data Analytics growth through 2031 is $5.30 a share: one Montana-sized contract a year, or 40 fleet sites upgrading to full conditioning, or the XSPCT fleet reaching 300 units. Management has said all three are in motion.

The bear case is $17. Estimates hold but the stock de-rates to the peer range: 11x consensus 2027 EBITDA of $65M, less $46M of net debt, over 38.4M diluted shares. That is where FTK trades if the market decides it is a chemical supplier with a sideline, which is what it was until 2025. The stress case, $40M of EBITDA at 8.5x, is $8 and needs ProFrac to fail.

Peers. RankedStocks ranks FTK first in its peer group with an overall score of 86.5: 83.6 on growth, 70.5 on profitability, 96.4 on sentiment and 95.0 on outlook. Valuation is the weak score at 12.2. The specialty-chemistry names, Stepan [], Innospec, Avient [] and Quaker Houghton [], score 37-47 on valuation with 4-7% forward revenue growth. The frac-exposed names score cheaper and grow slower: Halliburton 27.8, SLB 17.4 and ProFrac 79.9 on valuation, with 3-6% forward growth. Solaris scores 2.7 for 30.4% growth, and Kodiak Gas Services, the compression and power-rental name, scores 15.8 for 16.9% growth and a 29.7% forward EBIT margin. FTK’s 11.6% forward revenue growth and 10.7% forward EBIT margin put it between the chemistry group and the power renters, and its valuation score of 12.2 sits with Solaris and Kodiak. The market already pays for part of the power story, which is why my bear case de-rates FTK to the chemistry multiple.

Thirteen analysts cover FTK, seven at Buy and six at Hold, with a consensus target of $34.50 and a high of $44 (the ratings and targets are in the scorecard section). My $40 sits above the consensus and below the high, so the gap sits in the multiple the market will pay once the Puerto Rico noise is twelve months old.

If this changed how you look at the oilfield power trade, send it to the one person you argue with about data-center power.

Share

Verdict

BUY, with a fair value of $40 a share and a $17 bear case: 2.3x reward to risk, above the 2x I want before I buy.

FTK joins the portfolio at 3.5%, the low end of the 3.5-5% range I use for every new position; I cap even my strongest ideas at 5%.

It sits at the low end for three reasons: the controlling shareholder is levered, the stock carries a 25% short interest on a 15M-share float, so a headline moves it 20% in a day, and the ProFrac receivable still has to turn into cash.

It is a different way to own two themes already in the portfolio. The MENA oilfield services pick pays us to help the lowest-cost producer grow gas volumes; FTK supplies the chemistry inside the same Jafurah fleets. The infrastructure names pay us for the AI power build-out, and I laid out where that money lands in AI Capex: A 5-Question Energy Audit; FTK is the measurement and fuel-conditioning layer that the gas-fired half of the build-out needs.

The Q3 print on November 3 answers two questions: did the second-half Saudi shipments land, and did the $71M ProFrac receivable turn into cash.

A short seller priced a contract that produced no revenue; the company then raised guidance on the contracts that do.
truncated_body_text: A small cap with two businesses the market can’t price together: a 40-year-old industrial franchise that grew into a shrinking market, and a measurement-and-power platform that is 17% of revenue and half of gross profit. The short sellers got their 20% day. I think they got the wrong company.
